{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_7373a5e70ae74cc59d6e87925ef7ffcc",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/hosted-api-regional-failover-runbook.json",
    "title": "Runbook: Hosted API Regional Failover (On-Call)",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Runbook: Hosted API Regional Failover (On-Call)\",\n  \"space\": \"eng-sre\",\n  \"author\": \"Tom\\u00e1\\u0161 Nov\\u00e1k\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-12\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-10\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Rafael Mendes\",\n    \"Miles Thornton\",\n    \"Mina Haddad\",\n    \"Victor Alvarez\",\n    \"Allison Grant\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"runbook\",\n    \"hosted-api\",\n    \"failover\",\n    \"multi-region\",\n    \"sre\",\n    \"routing\",\n    \"incident-response\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/regional-failover-automation-upgrade-overview\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-042-failover-trigger-signal-hierarchy\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-043-automated-routing-policy-rollback\",\n    \"confluence://eng-platform/systems-and-services/region-health-service\",\n    \"confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/failover-signal-dashboards-spec\",\n    \"confluence://oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/regional-failover-communication-playbook\",\n    \"confluence://oncall-and-incident-response/status-page-and-comms/status-page-template-regional-event\",\n    \"confluence://eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"## Purpose\\nThis runbook describes the on-call procedure for executing (or approving) **Hosted API** regional failover during a real regional impairment or a controlled test. It covers triage, validation of trigger signals, initiating automation (including dry-run), monitoring during traffic shift, rollback, and post-event verification.\\n\\n**Primary goal:** reduce customer-visible impact by failing over quickly when the region is actually impaired, while avoiding false positives and oscillation.\\n\\n## Audience\\n- SRE On-Call (primary)\\n- Routing/Smart Routing On-Call (secondary)\\n- Network On-Call (as needed)\\n- Control Plane On-Call (as needed)\\n\\n## Definitions\\n- **Primary region:** currently preferred region for a Hosted API route/model group (e.g., `us-east` for most NA traffic).\\n- **Failover:** shifting eligible traffic from an impaired region to one or more healthy regions via routing policy updates.\\n- **Regional impairment:** region-level loss of reachability and/or sustained service-level failure (e.g., elevated 5xx burn) consistent across multiple independent signals.\\n- **Partial degradation:** single model pool, single AZ, or a dependency issue not requiring region-wide failover.\\n\\n## Preconditions / Safety\\n1) Confirm this is **Hosted API** traffic (not Dedicated-only). If Dedicated is impacted, coordinate separately per Dedicated runbooks.\\n2) Ensure you have the correct scope:\\n   - Which **route(s)**: `chat.completions`, `responses`, `embeddings`, etc.\\n   - Which **model group(s)**: `rw-llama-70b`, `rw-qwen-32b`, etc.\\n   - Which **tenant tier(s)** impacted: `free`, `pro`, `enterprise`.\\n3) Review automation mode for production:\\n   - **Dry-run** is always permitted.\\n   - **Execute** may require approval hooks depending on the route/tier configuration.\\n4) Data residency constraints: some enterprise tenants have region pinning. Failover must respect constraints (see \\u201cDo Not Fail Over\\u201d section and Security guidance).\\n\\n## Signals and Trigger Hierarchy (Summary)\\nThe authoritative prioritization is defined in **[ADR-042: Failover Trigger Signal Hierarchy]**.\\n\\nUse this simplified hierarchy when making a decision:\\n1) **Reachability loss** (cross-region probes + edge reachability) \\n2) **5xx burn-rate** for Hosted API (multi-window burn confirmation)\\n3) **Tail latency burn-rate** (P95/P99) with corroborating errors or reachability\\n4) **Capacity exhaustion / headroom collapse** (sustained) that cannot be mitigated by local scaling\\n\\n**Corroboration rule (operational):** do not execute production failover based on a single signal unless it is clearly reachability loss across multiple probe sources.\\n\\n## Required Dashboards / Links\\nRefer to **[Failover Signal Dashboards Spec]** for panel names and interpretations. Minimum set before executing:\\n- Region Health Summary (aggregated): `region-health-service` view\\n- Hosted API Availability: 2xx/4xx/5xx rate by region + route\\n- Burn-rate alerts: 5m/1h multi-window burn for multi-region availability SLO\\n- Tail latency by region: p95/p99 for key routes\\n- Capacity headroom by region: GPU queue depth, available tokens/sec, batcher saturation\\n- Routing policy flips timeline + audit events\\n- Cross-region probe results (perf-canary reachability/latency)\\n\\n## Tools\\n### Failover Controller CLI\\nUse the internal failover controller CLI to inspect, simulate, and (if permitted) execute changes.\\n\\nCommon commands (examples):\\n- Inspect current state:\\n  - `rwi-failoverctl status --service hosted-api --region us-east`\\n- Review signals / evidence:\\n  - `rwi-failoverctl evidence --service hosted-api --region us-east --window 30m`\\n- Dry-run (recommended actions only):\\n  - `rwi-failoverctl recommend --service hosted-api --from us-east --to eu-west --dry-run`\\n- Execute (requires approval hook in some prod configs):\\n  - `rwi-failoverctl execute --service hosted-api --from us-east --to eu-west --reason \\\"region impairment\\\"`\\n- Rollback:\\n  - `rwi-failoverctl rollback --service hosted-api --change-id <id> --reason \\\"region recovered\\\"`\\n\\nNotes:\\n- All dry-run and execute actions emit an audit event (see \\u201cAuditability\\u201d below).\\n- If the CLI cannot reach the controller/control plane, coordinate with Control Plane On-Call and consider manual routing policy change only as a last resort.\\n\\n### Incident-bot integration\\nThe failover controller posts summaries on trigger/recommend/execute/rollback. If missing, post manually with the template in \\u201cComms\\u201d.\\n\\n## Severity / When to Initiate Failover\\nInitiate failover actions when **either**:\\n- You see a page for regional impairment (reachability + service impact), or\\n- Multiple customers report elevated 5xx/timeouts correlated to a single region, or\\n- Burn-rate alert triggers for multi-region availability and is clearly tied to one region.\\n\\nIf impact is limited to a single route/model pool and can be mitigated locally (restart, scale, drain bad nodes), prefer local mitigation first.\\n\\n## Step-by-step Procedure\\n### 1) Triage and confirm it\\u2019s regional\\n1. Open incident channel and assign roles:\\n   - Incident Commander (IC): SRE On-Call unless escalated\\n   - Routing liaison: Smart Routing On-Call\\n   - Network liaison: Network On-Call if reachability suspected\\n   - Observability support: optional\\n2. Confirm symptoms:\\n   - Customer impact: 5xx spikes, timeouts, elevated p99, streaming disconnects\\n   - Scope: specific region (`us-east`) vs global\\n3. Check Region Health Summary:\\n   - Is `us-east` marked `DEGRADED` or `UNHEALTHY`?\\n   - Which signals contributed (reachability, 5xx burn, latency burn, capacity)?\\n4. Validate reachability:\\n   - Cross-region probes: `eu-west -> us-east`, `us-west -> us-east`\\n   - Edge reachability: client ingress success rate in region\\n   - Network indicators: packet loss, BGP/anycast anomalies (if applicable)\\n5. Validate service-level impact:\\n   - Hosted API 5xx rate by region/route\\n   - Burn-rate: confirm multi-window (fast + slow) windows are both elevated to avoid false positives\\n   - Tail latency: verify not caused solely by client retry storms\\n6. Validate capacity/headroom:\\n   - GPU pool saturation, queue depth\\n   - Autoscaler events and whether capacity can recover within minutes\\n\\nDecision checkpoint:\\n- If signals indicate **localized service issue** (single model, single AZ, single dependency), do not fail over region-wide yet. Escalate to service owner and mitigate locally.\\n- If signals indicate **region impairment**, proceed to dry-run.\\n\\n### 2) Dry-run failover recommendation (required before execute)\\n1. Run dry-run recommendation:\\n   - `rwi-failoverctl recommend --service hosted-api --from us-east --to <candidate> --dry-run`\\n2. Review output for:\\n   - Recommended destination region(s) and weights\\n   - Evidence list (signals, timestamps, confidence)\\n   - Guardrails that will apply (rate limits, hold-down timers, per-tenant safety)\\n3. Validate destination readiness:\\n   - Capacity headroom meets \\u201csafe to failover\\u201d criteria for the affected routes/models\\n   - No concurrent degradation in destination\\n   - Tail latency acceptable under projected load\\n4. Confirm \\u201cDo Not Fail Over\\u201d constraints:\\n   - Data residency pinned tenants cannot be shifted (ensure policy respects pinning)\\n   - Known incompatibilities: model version parity, feature flags, or region-specific dependencies\\n\\nIf the dry-run suggests \\u201chold / no action\\u201d due to insufficient corroboration or guardrails, do not force execute without Routing lead approval.\\n\\n### 3) Approval and execute\\nDepending on route/tier, production execute may require explicit approval.\\n\\n1. Announce intent in incident channel:\\n   - Source region, destination region(s)\\n   - Current impact (5xx/latency)\\n   - Signals justifying failover\\n   - Expected blast radius and rollback trigger\\n2. If approval hook is enabled:\\n   - Request approval from designated approver (usually SRE IC + Routing On-Call; enterprise scope may require SRE Manager)\\n3. Execute failover:\\n   - `rwi-failoverctl execute --service hosted-api --from us-east --to eu-west --reason \\\"<ticket/incident + summary>\\\"`\\n4. Confirm controller actions:\\n   - Routing policy updated\\n   - Circuit breakers / backpressure settings applied (if part of the workflow)\\n   - Audit event emitted with change-id\\n\\n### 4) Monitor during traffic shift (first 15 minutes are critical)\\nWatch these panels continuously:\\n1. Customer-visible impact:\\n   - Overall 5xx rate (global)\\n   - Route-level error rate for key endpoints\\n   - Streaming stability metrics (disconnect/reconnect)\\n2. Destination region health:\\n   - GPU queue depth / saturation\\n   - P95/P99 latency\\n   - Retry-after responses (should increase under overload rather than hard timeouts)\\n3. Failover side effects:\\n   - Thundering herd (retry spikes)\\n   - Elevated tail latency due to cache misses / cold KV cache\\n   - Unexpected auth/control-plane errors\\n\\nIf destination starts to degrade:\\n- Engage load shedding controls (per gateway defaults) and consider partial failover (reduce weights) instead of full shift.\\n- Coordinate with Routing On-Call to adjust weights or add an additional destination.\\n\\n### 5) Customer impact checks\\n1. Confirm representative customer success:\\n   - Sample synthetic requests from multiple geos\\n   - Check top enterprise tenants dashboards (if available) for elevated errors\\n2. If customer tickets are open (Support), provide:\\n   - Current status (mitigating via regional failover)\\n   - Expected behavior (brief transient errors, possible streaming reconnect)\\n   - Workaround guidance (retry with exponential backoff; honor Retry-After)\\n\\n### 6) Stabilization and decision to hold vs rollback\\nHold-down timers and anti-flap rules are defined in **[ADR-043]** and enforced by the controller. Operationally:\\n\\nRollback only when:\\n- Source region signals are healthy for the required stability window, AND\\n- Destination region is stable, AND\\n- You have a plan for a safe traffic return (gradual weights preferred)\\n\\nPrefer **gradual rollback** (weighted return) to avoid oscillation.\\n\\n### 7) Rollback procedure\\n1. Run rollback dry-run:\\n   - `rwi-failoverctl recommend --service hosted-api --from eu-west --to us-east --dry-run`\\n2. If recommended and stable, execute rollback:\\n   - `rwi-failoverctl rollback --service hosted-api --change-id <id> --reason \\\"region recovered\\\"`\\n3. Monitor for at least 30 minutes after rollback:\\n   - Error rate and latency in both regions\\n   - Policy flip rate (ensure no repeated flaps)\\n\\n## Do Not Fail Over (Common False-Positive Scenarios)\\nDo not execute a region-wide failover if the issue is likely:\\n- A single model deployment regression in-region (roll back model/version instead)\\n- Control plane impairment affecting policy distribution (failover may not apply cleanly)\\n- A global dependency outage (auth, billing, shared datastore) where failover doesn\\u2019t help\\n- Client-side retry storms causing latency (tune retries/backoff; use Retry-After)\\n- Destination region lacks sufficient headroom or is already degraded\\n- Tenant data residency pinning prevents safe cross-region routing\\n\\nWhen unsure, escalate to:\\n- Routing On-Call (policy semantics, partial failover)\\n- Network On-Call (reachability signal validation)\\n- Control Plane On-Call (controller health)\\n\\n## Auditability / Evidence Collection\\nEvery recommendation/execute/rollback should be traceable:\\n- Capture the controller change-id in the incident timeline\\n- Link dashboards used to make the decision (Region Health Summary, burn panels)\\n- Ensure audit event exists (used for enterprise audit requests)\\n\\nIf audit events are missing:\\n- Record the exact commands run and timestamps\\n- File a ticket with the failover controller team (include incident id)\\n\\n## Communication Checklist\\nFollow **[Regional Failover Communication Playbook]**.\\n\\nMinimum internal comms:\\n- Update incident channel with:\\n  - What is failing (region + symptoms)\\n  - What we did (dry-run, execute, weights)\\n  - What to watch (destination headroom, burn)\\n\\nStatus page (if customer-visible impact exceeds thresholds):\\n- Use **[Status Page Template: Regional Event]**\\n- Update cadence: every 15\\u201330 minutes while actively mitigating\\n- Ensure wording distinguishes \\u201cregional impairment\\u201d from \\u201cplanned test\\u201d\\n\\nIncident-bot manual template (if automation posts fail):\\n- \\\"Failover action: shifted Hosted API traffic from <from> to <to>. Reason: <reachability/5xx burn/latency burn/capacity>. Change-id: <id>. Monitoring: <dashboard link>. Rollback trigger: <criteria>.\\\"\\n\\n## Post-event Validation (Closeout)\\nWithin 1 hour of stabilization:\\n1. Confirm SLO impact snapshot:\\n   - Multi-region availability SLO burn during the window\\n   - Peak 5xx and duration\\n2. Confirm client experience:\\n   - Streaming reconnect metrics improved\\n   - Retry-after usage (no prolonged hard timeouts)\\n3. Confirm operational hygiene:\\n   - Controller did not flap (flip rate within limits)\\n   - Alerts returned to green and are not noisy\\n4. Create follow-ups:\\n   - Any signal gaps (missing probe, delayed burn alert)\\n   - Any dashboard gaps (missing annotations)\\n   - Any guardrails needed (rate limits, hold-down tuning)\\n\\n## Escalation / Ownership\\n- SRE On-Call: owns incident coordination and decision to execute/rollback\\n- Routing On-Call (Smart Routing): owns policy semantics, weights, constraints\\n- Network On-Call: validates reachability anomalies and provider symptoms\\n- Observability: dashboards/alert correctness\\n\\nIf repeated flapping or unclear signals occur, escalate to:\\n- Miles Thornton (Failover architecture lead)\\n- Rafael Mendes (SRE delivery lead)\\n\\n## Appendix A: Quick Validation Queries (Examples)\\nUse these as mental checklists (exact query syntax varies by dashboard):\\n- 5xx rate by region and route over last 10m vs 1h\\n- Burn-rate: fast window (5m) and slow window (1h) both elevated\\n- Cross-region probes: `success_rate < 95%` and/or latency step-change\\n- Destination headroom: sustained queue depth below alert threshold and autoscaler not maxed\\n\\n## Appendix B: Controlled Test Notes\\nFor planned game days:\\n- Always run in a limited blast radius configuration (approved tenants/routes)\\n- Announce start/end in #eng-sre and #support with explicit customer comms plan\\n- Use dry-run first, then execute with pre-agreed rollback triggers\\n- Ensure dashboards have automation annotations enabled before start\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_7373a5e70ae74cc59d6e87925ef7ffcc\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Runbook: Hosted API Regional Failover (On-Call)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/hosted-api-regional-failover-runbook.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: eng-sre\n\n- call ( secondary ) - network on - call ( as needed ) - control plane on - call ( as needed ) # # definitions - * * primary region : * * currently preferred region for a hosted api route / model group ( e. g., ` us - east ` for most na traffic ). - * * failover : * * shifting eligible traffic from an impaired region to one or more healthy regions via routing policy updates. - * * regional impairment : * * region - level loss of reachability and / or sustained service - level failure ( e. g., elevated 5xx burn ) consistent across multiple independent signals. - * * partial degradation : * * single model pool, single az, or a dependency issue not requiring region - wide failover.",

    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-042-failover-trigger-signal-hierarchy",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-043-automated-routing-policy-rollback",
    "confluence://eng-platform/systems-and-services/region-health-service",
    "confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/failover-signal-dashboards-spec",
    "confluence://oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/regional-failover-communication-playbook",
    "confluence://oncall-and-incident-response/status-page-and-comms/status-page-template-regional-event",
    "confluence://eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-pool-drain-and-evacuation-procedure"
  ],
  "content": "## Purpose
This runbook describes the on-call procedure for executing (or approving) **Hosted API** regional failover during a real regional impairment or a controlled test. It covers triage, validation of trigger signals, initiating automation (including dry-run), monitoring during traffic shift, rollback, and post-event verification.

**Primary goal:** reduce customer-visible impact by failing over quickly when the region is actually impaired, while avoiding false positives and oscillation.

## Audience
- SRE On-Call (primary)
- Routing/Smart Routing On-Call (secondary)
- Network On-Call (as needed)
- Control Plane On-Call (as needed)

## Definitions
- **Primary region:** currently preferred region for a Hosted API route/model group (e.g., `us-east` for most NA traffic).
- **Failover:** shifting eligible traffic from an impaired region to one or more healthy regions via routing policy updates.
- **Regional impairment:** region-level loss of reachability and/or sustained service-level failure (e.g., elevated 5xx burn) consistent across multiple independent signals.
- **Partial degradation:** single model pool, single AZ, or a dependency issue not requiring region-wide failover.

## Preconditions / Safety
1) Confirm this is **Hosted API** traffic (not Dedicated-only). If Dedicated is impacted, coordinate separately per Dedicated runbooks.
2) Ensure you have the correct scope:
   - Which **route(s)**: `chat.completions`, `responses`, `embeddings`, etc.
   - Which **model group(s)**: `rw-llama-70b`, `rw-qwen-32b`, etc.
   - Which **tenant tier(s)** impacted: `free`, `pro`, `enterprise`.
3) Review automation mode for production:
   - **Dry-run** is always permitted.
   - **Execute** may require approval hooks depending on the route/tier configuration.
4) Data residency constraints: some enterprise tenants have region pinning. Failover must respect constraints (see “Do Not Fail Over” section and Security guidance).

## Signals and Trigger Hierarchy (Summary)
The authoritative prioritization is defined in **[ADR-042: Failover Trigger Signal Hierarchy]**.

Use this simplified hierarchy when making a decision:
1) **Reachability loss** (cross-region probes + edge reachability) 
2) **5xx burn-rate** for Hosted API (multi-window burn confirmation)
3) **Tail latency burn-rate** (P95/P99) with corroborating errors or reachability
4) **Capacity exhaustion / headroom collapse** (sustained) that cannot be mitigated by local scaling

**Corroboration rule (operational):** do not execute production failover based on a single signal unless it is clearly reachability loss across multiple probe sources.

## Required Dashboards / Links
Refer to **[Failover Signal Dashboards Spec]** for panel names and interpretations. Minimum set before executing:
- Region Health Summary (aggregated): `region-health-service` view
- Hosted API Availability: 2xx/4xx/5xx rate by region + route
- Burn-rate alerts: 5m/1h multi-window burn for multi-region availability SLO
- Tail latency by region: p95/p99 for key routes
- Capacity headroom by region: GPU queue depth, available tokens/sec, batcher saturation
- Routing policy flips timeline + audit events
- Cross-region probe results (perf-canary reachability/latency)

## Tools
### Failover Controller CLI
Use the internal failover controller CLI to inspect, simulate, and (if permitted) execute changes.

Common commands (examples):
- Inspect current state:
  - `rwi-failoverctl status --service hosted-api --region us-east`
- Review signals / evidence:
  - `rwi-failoverctl evidence --service hosted-api --region us-east --window 30m`
- Dry-run (recommended actions only):
  - `rwi-failoverctl recommend --service hosted-api --from us-east --to eu-west --dry-run`
- Execute (requires approval hook in some prod configs):
  - `rwi-failoverctl execute --service hosted-api --from us-east --to eu-west --reason "region impairment"`
- Rollback:
  - `rwi-failoverctl rollback --service hosted-api --change-id <id> --reason "region recovered"`

Notes:
- All dry-run and execute actions emit an audit event (see “Auditability” below).
- If the CLI cannot reach the controller/control plane, coordinate with Control Plane On-Call and consider manual routing policy change only as a last resort.

### Incident-bot integration
The failover controller posts summaries on trigger/recommend/execute/rollback. If missing, post manually with the template in “Comms”.

## Severity / When to Initiate Failover
Initiate failover actions when **either**:
- You see a page for regional impairment (reachability + service impact), or
- Multiple customers report elevated 5xx/timeouts correlated to a single region, or
- Burn-rate alert triggers for multi-region availability and is clearly tied to one region.

If impact is limited to a single route/model pool and can be mitigated locally (restart, scale, drain bad nodes), prefer local mitigation first.

## Step-by-step Procedure
### 1) Triage and confirm it’s regional
1. Open incident channel and assign roles:
   - Incident Commander (IC): SRE On-Call unless escalated
   - Routing liaison: Smart Routing On-Call
   - Network liaison: Network On-Call if reachability suspected
   - Observability support: optional
2. Confirm symptoms:
   - Customer impact: 5xx spikes, timeouts, elevated p99, streaming disconnects
   - Scope: specific region (`us-east`) vs global
3. Check Region Health Summary:
   - Is `us-east` marked `DEGRADED` or `UNHEALTHY`?
   - Which signals contributed (reachability, 5xx burn, latency burn, capacity)?
4. Validate reachability:
   - Cross-region probes: `eu-west -> us-east`, `us-west -> us-east`
   - Edge reachability: client ingress success rate in region
   - Network indicators: packet loss, BGP/anycast anomalies (if applicable)
5. Validate service-level impact:
   - Hosted API 5xx rate by region/route
   - Burn-rate: confirm multi-window (fast + slow) windows are both elevated to avoid false positives
   - Tail latency: verify not caused solely by client retry storms
6. Validate capacity/headroom:
   - GPU pool saturation, queue depth
   - Autoscaler events and whether capacity can recover within minutes

Decision checkpoint:
- If signals indicate **localized service issue** (single model, single AZ, single dependency), do not fail over region-wide yet. Escalate to service owner and mitigate locally.
- If signals indicate **region impairment**, proceed to dry-run.

### 2) Dry-run failover recommendation (required before execute)
1. Run dry-run recommendation:
   - `rwi-failoverctl recommend --service hosted-api --from us-east --to <candidate> --dry-run`
2. Review output for:
   - Recommended destination region(s) and weights
   - Evidence list (signals, timestamps, confidence)
   - Guardrails that will apply (rate limits, hold-down timers, per-tenant safety)
3. Validate destination readiness:
   - Capacity headroom meets “safe to failover” criteria for the affected routes/models
   - No concurrent degradation in destination
   - Tail latency acceptable under projected load
4. Confirm “Do Not Fail Over” constraints:
   - Data residency pinned tenants cannot be shifted (ensure policy respects pinning)
   - Known incompatibilities: model version parity, feature flags, or region-specific dependencies

If the dry-run suggests “hold / no action” due to insufficient corroboration or guardrails, do not force execute without Routing lead approval.

### 3) Approval and execute
Depending on route/tier, production execute may require explicit approval.

1. Announce intent in incident channel:
   - Source region, destination region(s)
   - Current impact (5xx/latency)
   - Signals justifying failover
   - Expected blast radius and rollback trigger
2. If approval hook is enabled:
   - Request approval from designated approver (usually SRE IC + Routing On-Call; enterprise scope may require SRE Manager)
3. Execute failover:
   - `rwi-failoverctl execute --service hosted-api --from us-east --to eu-west --reason "<ticket/incident + summary>"`
4. Confirm controller actions:
   - Routing policy updated
   - Circuit breakers / backpressure settings applied (if part of the workflow)
   - Audit event emitted with change-id

### 4) Monitor during traffic shift (first 15 minutes are critical)
Watch these panels continuously:
1. Customer-visible impact:
   - Overall 5xx rate (global)
   - Route-level error rate for key endpoints
   - Streaming stability metrics (disconnect/reconnect)
2. Destination region health:
   - GPU queue depth / saturation
   - P95/P99 latency
   - Retry-after responses (should increase under overload rather than hard timeouts)
3. Failover side effects:
   - Thundering herd (retry spikes)
   - Elevated tail latency due to cache misses / cold KV cache
   - Unexpected auth/control-plane errors

If destination starts to degrade:
- Engage load shedding controls (per gateway defaults) and consider partial failover (reduce weights) instead of full shift.
- Coordinate with Routing On-Call to adjust weights or add an additional destination.

### 5) Customer impact checks
1. Confirm representative customer success:
   - Sample synthetic requests from multiple geos
   - Check top enterprise tenants dashboards (if available) for elevated errors
2. If customer tickets are open (Support), provide:
   - Current status (mitigating via regional failover)
   - Expected behavior (brief transient errors, possible streaming reconnect)
   - Workaround guidance (retry with exponential backoff; honor Retry-After)

### 6) Stabilization and decision to hold vs rollback
Hold-down timers and anti-flap rules are defined in **[ADR-043]** and enforced by the controller. Operationally:

Rollback only when:
- Source region signals are healthy for the required stability window, AND
- Destination region is stable, AND
- You have a plan for a safe traffic return (gradual weights preferred)

Prefer **gradual rollback** (weighted return) to avoid oscillation.

### 7) Rollback procedure
1. Run rollback dry-run:
   - `rwi-failoverctl recommend --service hosted-api --from eu-west --to us-east --dry-run`
2. If recommended and stable, execute rollback:
   - `rwi-failoverctl rollback --service hosted-api --change-id <id> --reason "region recovered"`
3. Monitor for at least 30 minutes after rollback:
   - Error rate and latency in both regions
   - Policy flip rate (ensure no repeated flaps)

## Do Not Fail Over (Common False-Positive Scenarios)
Do not execute a region-wide failover if the issue is likely:
- A single model deployment regression in-region (roll back model/version instead)
- Control plane impairment affecting policy distribution (failover may not apply cleanly)
- A global dependency outage (auth, billing, shared datastore) where failover doesn’t help
- Client-side retry storms causing latency (tune retries/backoff; use Retry-After)
- Destination region lacks sufficient headroom or is already degraded
- Tenant data residency pinning prevents safe cross-region routing

When unsure, escalate to:
- Routing On-Call (policy semantics, partial failover)
- Network On-Call (reachability signal validation)
- Control Plane On-Call (controller health)

## Auditability / Evidence Collection
Every recommendation/execute/rollback should be traceable:
- Capture the controller change-id in the incident timeline
- Link dashboards used to make the decision (Region Health Summary, burn panels)
- Ensure audit event exists (used for enterprise audit requests)

If audit events are missing:
- Record the exact commands run and timestamps
- File a ticket with the failover controller team (include incident id)

## Communication Checklist
Follow **[Regional Failover Communication Playbook]**.

Minimum internal comms:
- Update incident channel with:
  - What is failing (region + symptoms)
  - What we did (dry-run, execute, weights)
  - What to watch (destination headroom, burn)

Status page (if customer-visible impact exceeds thresholds):
- Use **[Status Page Template: Regional Event]**
- Update cadence: every 15–30 minutes while actively mitigating
- Ensure wording distinguishes “regional impairment” from “planned test”

Incident-bot manual template (if automation posts fail):
- "Failover action: shifted Hosted API traffic from <from> to <to>. Reason: <reachability/5xx burn/latency burn/capacity>. Change-id: <id>. Monitoring: <dashboard link>. Rollback trigger: <criteria>."

## Post-event Validation (Closeout)
Within 1 hour of stabilization:
1. Confirm SLO impact snapshot:
   - Multi-region availability SLO burn during the window
   - Peak 5xx and duration
2. Confirm client experience:
   - Streaming reconnect metrics improved
   - Retry-after usage (no prolonged hard timeouts)
3. Confirm operational hygiene:
   - Controller did not flap (flip rate within limits)
   - Alerts returned to green and are not noisy
4. Create follow-ups:
   - Any signal gaps (missing probe, delayed burn alert)
   - Any dashboard gaps (missing annotations)
   - Any guardrails needed (rate limits, hold-down tuning)

## Escalation / Ownership
- SRE On-Call: owns incident coordination and decision to execute/rollback
- Routing On-Call (Smart Routing): owns policy semantics, weights, constraints
- Network On-Call: validates reachability anomalies and provider symptoms
- Observability: dashboards/alert correctness

If repeated flapping or unclear signals occur, escalate to:
- Miles Thornton (Failover architecture lead)
- Rafael Mendes (SRE delivery lead)

## Appendix A: Quick Validation Queries (Examples)
Use these as mental checklists (exact query syntax varies by dashboard):
- 5xx rate by region and route over last 10m vs 1h
- Burn-rate: fast window (5m) and slow window (1h) both elevated
- Cross-region probes: `success_rate < 95%` and/or latency step-change
- Destination headroom: sustained queue depth below alert threshold and autoscaler not maxed

## Appendix B: Controlled Test Notes
For planned game days:
- Always run in a limited blast radius configuration (approved tenants/routes)
- Announce start/end in #eng-sre and #support with explicit customer comms plan
- Use dry-run first, then execute with pre-agreed rollback triggers
- Ensure dashboards have automation annotations enabled before start

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Hosted Data Residency Enforcement (Region Pinning) \\u2014 Sales & Security FAQ\",\n  \"space\": \"sales-enablement\",\n  \"author\": \"Elliot Price\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"go-to-market\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"confidentiality\": \"restricted\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-02-10\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2025-03-04\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Naomi Feldman\",\n    \"Marcus Lin\",\n    \"Dr. Aisha Rahman\",\n    \"Olga Petrov\",\n    \"Markus Klein\",\n    \"Sean Gallagher\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"security-faq\",\n    \"data-residency\",\n    \"enterprise\",\n    \"hosted-api\",\n    \"region-pinning\",\n    \"audit-logs\",\n    \"routing\",\n    \"support\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://product-docs/requirements/hosted-data-residency-enforcement-prd\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-021-region-pinning-enforcement-boundaries\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-022-error-contract-for-residency-violations\",\n    \"confluence://security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/hosted-data-residency-policy-and-controls\",\n    \"confluence://eng-platform/systems-and-services/residency-policy-service\"\n  ],\n  \"body\": \"## Purpose\\nThis FAQ equips Sales, Solutions Engineering, and Security reviewers to answer common questions about **Hosted data residency enforcement** (also referred to as **region pinning**) for the Redwood Hosted API, and how behavior differs for **Dedicated** and **Private** deployments.\\n\\nThis document is intended for internal enablement. You may quote approved excerpts to customers, but do not forward the full page externally.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Executive summary (customer-facing)\\n- Customers can configure an **allowed region set** (e.g., **EU-only**) and a **primary region** for Redwood Hosted API processing.\\n- Redwood enforces residency **at request time** with deterministic checks. If a request would violate policy, it is **blocked** with a consistent error response (no silent cross-region processing).\\n- **Cross-region fallback is disabled by default** when residency pinning is enabled. Fallback is only permitted **within the allowed region set**.\\n- Redwood provides **auditability**: configuration change history, audit-log events for policy changes, and observability for blocked requests.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Definitions (use these consistently)\\n**Region pinning / residency policy**\\nA control-plane configuration that constrains where **customer content** for an org/project (and optionally an API key) may be processed.\\n\\n**Allowed regions**\\nThe set of regions where content processing is permitted (e.g., `eu-west`, `eu-central`).\\n\\n**Primary region**\\nThe default region used when multiple allowed regions exist.\\n\\n**Customer content**\\nInputs and outputs of inference and closely associated content-bearing artifacts, including (non-exhaustive):\\n- Prompts/messages, uploaded text, tool/function arguments that include customer data\\n- Model outputs/completions\\n- Embeddings payloads\\n- Fine-tuning/training data is out of scope for Hosted API (not offered as part of this feature)\\n\\n**Content-derived metadata**\\nDerived values such as token counts, latency, model name, error codes. These may be stored/processed as operational metadata (see Logging & observability).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Product scope & guarantees\\n### Q: What does Redwood guarantee for Hosted API with region pinning enabled?\\n**A:** When region pinning is enabled for a project/org, Redwood guarantees that customer content is:\\n- **Routed only to compute in the allowed region set**\\n- **Not processed in disallowed regions**, including during overload scenarios\\n- **Not silently failed over cross-region** (requests will be blocked instead)\\n- Handled such that in-scope logs/traces that include customer content are **kept within the pinned region boundary**\\n\\n### Q: What is explicitly not guaranteed in the initial release?\\n**A:** The initial release does not provide:\\n- Automatic multi-region replication of customer content\\n- Arbitrary per-endpoint residency rules for every internal subsystem (coverage is delivered via phased hardening)\\n- Customer-controlled selection of specific availability zones (AZ) within a region\\n\\n### Q: Which Redwood products does this apply to?\\n**A:**\\n- **Hosted API:** Full feature scope (pinning + enforcement + error contract + observability + auditability)\\n- **Dedicated:** Similar concept (region selection and routing constraints) but deployment is already region-scoped by design; details depend on contract/SLA\\n- **Private (VPC/on-prem):** Residency is primarily controlled by the customer\\u2019s infrastructure and network boundaries; Redwood provides configuration support and guidance\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Configuration & policy precedence\\n### Q: At what level can customers configure region pinning?\\n**A:** Region pinning can be configured at:\\n- **Org** level (default policy)\\n- **Project** level (overrides org policy for that project)\\n- **API key** level (optional; used for staged migrations or exceptions)\\n\\n### Q: If multiple policies apply, which one wins?\\n**A:** Precedence is:\\n1) API key policy (most specific)\\n2) Project policy\\n3) Org policy\\n\\n### Q: Can customers restrict specific API keys to narrower regions than the overall org?\\n**A:** Yes. Example: Org allowed regions `EU`, but a specific API key restricted to `eu-west` only.\\n\\n### Q: Can customers set \\u201cEU-only\\u201d while still using a global endpoint hostname?\\n**A:** Yes. Customers can use the standard API hostname; routing evaluates residency policy and selects an allowed region. (Some customers prefer region-specific base URLs; that is supported where documented, but policy enforcement remains authoritative.)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Request-time enforcement & errors\\n### Q: What happens if a request would be routed to a disallowed region?\\n**A:** The request is **blocked** and returns a **residency violation** error response with:\\n- An HTTP status appropriate for policy enforcement (see Error contract below)\\n- A machine-readable `error_code`\\n- A human-readable message describing what policy was violated\\n- A `request_id` to help support trace the exact decision\\n\\n### Q: Is the failure deterministic (no partial processing)?\\n**A:** Yes. Enforcement happens before content is processed. If blocked, Redwood does not run inference for that request.\\n\\n### Q: What HTTP status code should customers expect?\\n**A:** Residency blocks return **HTTP 409 (Conflict)** with a structured error payload. (This is intentionally distinct from validation errors and capacity errors.)\\n\\n### Q: What error code should we reference in troubleshooting?\\n**A:** Use the residency-specific error code in customer guidance (example format):\\n- `RESIDENCY_POLICY_VIOLATION`\\n\\nSupport can request the `request_id` and the project/org identifier to locate the decision log.\\n\\n### Q: Will streaming endpoints return a standard residency error (not a generic 500)?\\n**A:** Yes. Streaming endpoints are required to surface the same residency violation error contract. If a customer reports generic 500s on streaming during enforcement, treat it as a bug and escalate to API Gateway on-call.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Routing & fallback behavior\\n### Q: How does region pinning affect fallback (capacity/region failover)?\\n**A:** With pinning enabled:\\n- **Cross-region fallback is disabled by default**\\n- Redwood may fallback **within the allowed region set** (e.g., from `eu-west` to `eu-central`) if both are allowed\\n- If no allowed region has capacity, the request may fail with a capacity error rather than violating residency\\n\\n### Q: Can customers allow cross-region fallback as an opt-in?\\n**A:** By default, no\\u2014policy is designed to be strict to meet regulated requirements. For exceptional cases, discuss alternatives (e.g., expand allowed region set, Dedicated capacity, or a contractual DR arrangement for Dedicated). Any exception requires Security + Product approval.\\n\\n### Q: Does Redwood move traffic between regions for performance reasons (latency-based routing)?\\n**A:** Not when it would violate the allowed region set. Within the allowed set, Redwood may route to meet latency/availability goals.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Data handling: logs, traces, analytics\\n### Q: Are prompts/completions stored?\\n**A:** By default, Redwood does not persist prompts/completions for general product analytics. Operational logging is minimized and is governed by data handling controls.\\n\\nIf a customer enables optional diagnostic logging features (where available), Redwood will ensure those logs remain within the allowed region boundary when residency is enabled.\\n\\n### Q: What telemetry is collected, and where is it processed?\\n**A:** Redwood collects operational metadata such as:\\n- Request timing (latency), token counts, model identifier, status code, error code\\n- Region selection decision metadata (policy evaluation results)\\n\\nWhen residency pinning is enabled:\\n- **Content-bearing telemetry** (if present) is kept within the allowed region boundary\\n- **Aggregated, non-content metrics** may be processed in centralized systems for fleet health (does not include customer prompts/completions)\\n\\n### Q: Do traces contain customer content?\\n**A:** Traces are designed to avoid customer content. If any content-bearing fields exist in a trace path, they are treated as in-scope for residency boundaries and must remain within allowed regions. The engineering standard is to keep traces content-free; enforcement treats content-bearing traces as restricted.\\n\\n### Q: Do audit logs include customer content?\\n**A:** Audit logs cover configuration and administrative actions (e.g., \\u201cresidency policy updated\\u201d) and should not include prompt/completion content.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Subprocessors & cloud regions\\n### Q: Which subprocessors are used for Hosted API, and are they region-bound?\\n**A:** Hosted API runs on major cloud infrastructure providers and regional services. When residency pinning is enabled, Redwood selects compute and in-scope supporting services in the allowed region(s).\\n\\nFor security reviews, provide:\\n- Redwood\\u2019s current subprocessor list (via Trust Center or Security team)\\n- Confirmation that processing for pinned workloads occurs in the configured region(s)\\n\\nIf a customer needs a named-region subprocessor attestation (e.g., \\u201cEU-only\\u201d), route the request to Security (GRC) for the approved statement.\\n\\n### Q: Are any third-party services used that might process customer content cross-region?\\n**A:** For pinned workloads, Redwood\\u2019s design requirement is that customer content does not leave the allowed region set. If a customer requests deep detail per subsystem, provide the formal policy/control mapping and offer a security review session.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private (how to explain)\\n### Q: How is Dedicated different from Hosted for residency?\\n**A:**\\n- **Hosted:** Multi-tenant control plane and shared serving fleet; residency is enforced by policy at request time.\\n- **Dedicated:** A dedicated GPU pool is provisioned in a specific region (and optionally multiple regions by contract). Residency is inherently simpler because compute is single-tenant and region-scoped.\\n\\nIf a customer requires strict \\u201cno shared control plane metadata outside the region,\\u201d Dedicated or Private may be the right fit depending on requirements.\\n\\n### Q: Does Dedicated ever do cross-region DR/failover?\\n**A:** Only if explicitly designed and contracted. Default Dedicated deployments are provisioned within an agreed region, and failover behavior is defined in the Dedicated architecture and customer SLA.\\n\\n### Q: How does Private (VPC/on-prem) affect residency?\\n**A:** Private deployments run inside the customer\\u2019s network boundary (VPC/on-prem). Residency is primarily enforced by where the customer deploys the system. Redwood provides:\\n- The same policy concepts (where applicable)\\n- Operational guidance, but the customer controls the physical/virtual location\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Compliance & evidence\\n### Q: What artifacts can we provide for audits / security questionnaires?\\n**A:** Common artifacts include:\\n- Data residency policy and controls narrative\\n- Architecture overview describing enforcement boundaries\\n- Audit log examples showing residency policy change events\\n- Screenshots or exports from dashboards showing blocked requests metrics (redacted)\\n\\nCoordinate with GRC (Olga Petrov) for approved auditor-facing packages.\\n\\n### Q: Does region pinning support SOC 2 / ISO 27001 narratives?\\n**A:** Yes. The feature is designed to map to common control expectations: access control, change management (audit logs), monitoring, and policy enforcement.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Customer troubleshooting (field playbook)\\n### Q: Customer enabled pinning and now requests are blocked. What should we check first?\\n**A:**\\n1) Confirm the configured **allowed region set** matches where the customer expects to run\\n2) Confirm the customer is using the correct **org/project** and API key\\n3) Ask for: `request_id`, timestamp, endpoint, and project ID\\n4) Check whether they configured a single region without capacity (recommend adding a second allowed region within the same residency boundary, e.g., `eu-west` + `eu-central`)\\n\\n### Q: Customer claims requests are being served outside the pinned region. What\\u2019s our response?\\n**A:**\\n- Ask for evidence: request IDs, timestamps, observed region headers (if available), and relevant logs\\n- Escalate to SRE + Routing: treat as a severity-appropriate incident because it may indicate a policy enforcement bug\\n\\n### Q: How should we position the trade-off between residency strictness and availability?\\n**A:** Use this framing:\\n- Strict residency policies may reduce failover options.\\n- Redwood prioritizes compliance by blocking instead of violating policy.\\n- If the customer needs both strict residency and higher availability, recommend:\\n  - Allowing multiple regions within the same residency boundary (e.g., multiple EU regions)\\n  - Dedicated capacity in-region\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Approved language snippets (for emails / questionnaires)\\n**1) One-liner**\\n\\u201cRedwood supports region pinning for Hosted API. When enabled, customer content is processed only in the configured allowed regions, and requests that would violate policy are blocked with a deterministic error (no silent cross-region failover).\\u201d\\n\\n**2) Logging/telemetry**\\n\\u201cFor pinned workloads, Redwood keeps content-bearing logs/traces within the allowed region boundary. Operational metrics are designed to avoid customer content and may be aggregated centrally for service health.\\u201d\\n\\n**3) Fallback behavior**\\n\\u201cCross-region fallback is disabled by default under residency pinning. Redwood may fall back only within the allowed region set; otherwise requests fail rather than violating residency policy.\\u201d\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Contacts / escalation\\n- Product (policy intent, customer commitments): **Naomi Feldman**\\n- Security Engineering (controls, threat model): **Marcus Lin**\\n- GRC / evidence / auditor packs: **Olga Petrov**\\n- Solutions Engineering (customer rollout planning): **Markus Klein**\\n- SRE (enforcement incidents / false positives): **Sean Gallagher**\\n\\nIf a customer requests contractual language, route to Legal/Deal Desk and include Security + Product on the thread.\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_261a4ade6f21403185d98805521b1e1d\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Hosted Data Residency Enforcement (Region Pinning) — Sales & Security FAQ\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/sales-enablement/security-faq/data-residency-enforcement-faq.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: sales-enablement\n\ninternal enablement. you may quote approved excerpts to customers, but do not forward the full page externally. - - - # # executive summary ( customer - facing ) - customers can configure an * * allowed region set * * ( e. g., * * eu - only * * ) and a * * primary region * * for redwood hosted api processing. - redwood enforces residency * * at request time * * with deterministic checks. if a request would violate policy, it is * * blocked * * with a consistent error response ( no silent cross - region processing ). - * * cross - region fallback is disabled by default * * when residency pinning is enabled. fallback is only permitted * * within the allowed region set * *. - redwood provides * * auditability * * : configuration change history, audit",

document.content:
{
  "title": "Hosted Data Residency Enforcement (Region Pinning) — Sales & Security FAQ",
  "space": "sales-enablement",
  "author": "Elliot Price",
  "owner_team": "go-to-market",
  "status": "published",
  "confidentiality": "restricted",
  "created_at": "2025-02-10",
  "last_updated": "2025-03-04",
  "reviewers": [
    "Naomi Feldman",
    "Marcus Lin",
    "Dr. Aisha Rahman",
    "Olga Petrov",
    "Markus Klein",
    "Sean Gallagher"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "security-faq",
    "data-residency",
    "enterprise",
    "hosted-api",
    "region-pinning",
    "audit-logs",
    "routing",
    "support"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://product-docs/requirements/hosted-data-residency-enforcement-prd",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-021-region-pinning-enforcement-boundaries",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-022-error-contract-for-residency-violations",
    "confluence://security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/hosted-data-residency-policy-and-controls",
    "confluence://eng-platform/systems-and-services/residency-policy-service"
  ],
  "body": "## Purpose
This FAQ equips Sales, Solutions Engineering, and Security reviewers to answer common questions about **Hosted data residency enforcement** (also referred to as **region pinning**) for the Redwood Hosted API, and how behavior differs for **Dedicated** and **Private** deployments.

This document is intended for internal enablement. You may quote approved excerpts to customers, but do not forward the full page externally.

---

## Executive summary (customer-facing)
- Customers can configure an **allowed region set** (e.g., **EU-only**) and a **primary region** for Redwood Hosted API processing.
- Redwood enforces residency **at request time** with deterministic checks. If a request would violate policy, it is **blocked** with a consistent error response (no silent cross-region processing).
- **Cross-region fallback is disabled by default** when residency pinning is enabled. Fallback is only permitted **within the allowed region set**.
- Redwood provides **auditability**: configuration change history, audit-log events for policy changes, and observability for blocked requests.

---

## Definitions (use these consistently)
**Region pinning / residency policy**
A control-plane configuration that constrains where **customer content** for an org/project (and optionally an API key) may be processed.

**Allowed regions**
The set of regions where content processing is permitted (e.g., `eu-west`, `eu-central`).

**Primary region**
The default region used when multiple allowed regions exist.

**Customer content**
Inputs and outputs of inference and closely associated content-bearing artifacts, including (non-exhaustive):
- Prompts/messages, uploaded text, tool/function arguments that include customer data
- Model outputs/completions
- Embeddings payloads
- Fine-tuning/training data is out of scope for Hosted API (not offered as part of this feature)

**Content-derived metadata**
Derived values such as token counts, latency, model name, error codes. These may be stored/processed as operational metadata (see Logging & observability).

---

## Product scope & guarantees
### Q: What does Redwood guarantee for Hosted API with region pinning enabled?
**A:** When region pinning is enabled for a project/org, Redwood guarantees that customer content is:
- **Routed only to compute in the allowed region set**
- **Not processed in disallowed regions**, including during overload scenarios
- **Not silently failed over cross-region** (requests will be blocked instead)
- Handled such that in-scope logs/traces that include customer content are **kept within the pinned region boundary**

### Q: What is explicitly not guaranteed in the initial release?
**A:** The initial release does not provide:
- Automatic multi-region replication of customer content
- Arbitrary per-endpoint residency rules for every internal subsystem (coverage is delivered via phased hardening)
- Customer-controlled selection of specific availability zones (AZ) within a region

### Q: Which Redwood products does this apply to?
**A:**
- **Hosted API:** Full feature scope (pinning + enforcement + error contract + observability + auditability)
- **Dedicated:** Similar concept (region selection and routing constraints) but deployment is already region-scoped by design; details depend on contract/SLA
- **Private (VPC/on-prem):** Residency is primarily controlled by the customer’s infrastructure and network boundaries; Redwood provides configuration support and guidance

---

## Configuration & policy precedence
### Q: At what level can customers configure region pinning?
**A:** Region pinning can be configured at:
- **Org** level (default policy)
- **Project** level (overrides org policy for that project)
- **API key** level (optional; used for staged migrations or exceptions)

### Q: If multiple policies apply, which one wins?
**A:** Precedence is:
1) API key policy (most specific)
2) Project policy
3) Org policy

### Q: Can customers restrict specific API keys to narrower regions than the overall org?
**A:** Yes. Example: Org allowed regions `EU`, but a specific API key restricted to `eu-west` only.

### Q: Can customers set “EU-only” while still using a global endpoint hostname?
**A:** Yes. Customers can use the standard API hostname; routing evaluates residency policy and selects an allowed region. (Some customers prefer region-specific base URLs; that is supported where documented, but policy enforcement remains authoritative.)

---

## Request-time enforcement & errors
### Q: What happens if a request would be routed to a disallowed region?
**A:** The request is **blocked** and returns a **residency violation** error response with:
- An HTTP status appropriate for policy enforcement (see Error contract below)
- A machine-readable `error_code`
- A human-readable message describing what policy was violated
- A `request_id` to help support trace the exact decision

### Q: Is the failure deterministic (no partial processing)?
**A:** Yes. Enforcement happens before content is processed. If blocked, Redwood does not run inference for that request.

### Q: What HTTP status code should customers expect?
**A:** Residency blocks return **HTTP 409 (Conflict)** with a structured error payload. (This is intentionally distinct from validation errors and capacity errors.)

### Q: What error code should we reference in troubleshooting?
**A:** Use the residency-specific error code in customer guidance (example format):
- `RESIDENCY_POLICY_VIOLATION`

Support can request the `request_id` and the project/org identifier to locate the decision log.

### Q: Will streaming endpoints return a standard residency error (not a generic 500)?
**A:** Yes. Streaming endpoints are required to surface the same residency violation error contract. If a customer reports generic 500s on streaming during enforcement, treat it as a bug and escalate to API Gateway on-call.

---

## Routing & fallback behavior
### Q: How does region pinning affect fallback (capacity/region failover)?
**A:** With pinning enabled:
- **Cross-region fallback is disabled by default**
- Redwood may fallback **within the allowed region set** (e.g., from `eu-west` to `eu-central`) if both are allowed
- If no allowed region has capacity, the request may fail with a capacity error rather than violating residency

### Q: Can customers allow cross-region fallback as an opt-in?
**A:** By default, no—policy is designed to be strict to meet regulated requirements. For exceptional cases, discuss alternatives (e.g., expand allowed region set, Dedicated capacity, or a contractual DR arrangement for Dedicated). Any exception requires Security + Product approval.

### Q: Does Redwood move traffic between regions for performance reasons (latency-based routing)?
**A:** Not when it would violate the allowed region set. Within the allowed set, Redwood may route to meet latency/availability goals.

---

## Data handling: logs, traces, analytics
### Q: Are prompts/completions stored?
**A:** By default, Redwood does not persist prompts/completions for general product analytics. Operational logging is minimized and is governed by data handling controls.

If a customer enables optional diagnostic logging features (where available), Redwood will ensure those logs remain within the allowed region boundary when residency is enabled.

### Q: What telemetry is collected, and where is it processed?
**A:** Redwood collects operational metadata such as:
- Request timing (latency), token counts, model identifier, status code, error code
- Region selection decision metadata (policy evaluation results)

When residency pinning is enabled:
- **Content-bearing telemetry** (if present) is kept within the allowed region boundary
- **Aggregated, non-content metrics** may be processed in centralized systems for fleet health (does not include customer prompts/completions)

### Q: Do traces contain customer content?
**A:** Traces are designed to avoid customer content. If any content-bearing fields exist in a trace path, they are treated as in-scope for residency boundaries and must remain within allowed regions. The engineering standard is to keep traces content-free; enforcement treats content-bearing traces as restricted.

### Q: Do audit logs include customer content?
**A:** Audit logs cover configuration and administrative actions (e.g., “residency policy updated”) and should not include prompt/completion content.

---

## Subprocessors & cloud regions
### Q: Which subprocessors are used for Hosted API, and are they region-bound?
**A:** Hosted API runs on major cloud infrastructure providers and regional services. When residency pinning is enabled, Redwood selects compute and in-scope supporting services in the allowed region(s).

For security reviews, provide:
- Redwood’s current subprocessor list (via Trust Center or Security team)
- Confirmation that processing for pinned workloads occurs in the configured region(s)

If a customer needs a named-region subprocessor attestation (e.g., “EU-only”), route the request to Security (GRC) for the approved statement.

### Q: Are any third-party services used that might process customer content cross-region?
**A:** For pinned workloads, Redwood’s design requirement is that customer content does not leave the allowed region set. If a customer requests deep detail per subsystem, provide the formal policy/control mapping and offer a security review session.

---

## Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private (how to explain)
### Q: How is Dedicated different from Hosted for residency?
**A:**
- **Hosted:** Multi-tenant control plane and shared serving fleet; residency is enforced by policy at request time.
- **Dedicated:** A dedicated GPU pool is provisioned in a specific region (and optionally multiple regions by contract). Residency is inherently simpler because compute is single-tenant and region-scoped.

If a customer requires strict “no shared control plane metadata outside the region,” Dedicated or Private may be the right fit depending on requirements.

### Q: Does Dedicated ever do cross-region DR/failover?
**A:** Only if explicitly designed and contracted. Default Dedicated deployments are provisioned within an agreed region, and failover behavior is defined in the Dedicated architecture and customer SLA.

### Q: How does Private (VPC/on-prem) affect residency?
**A:** Private deployments run inside the customer’s network boundary (VPC/on-prem). Residency is primarily enforced by where the customer deploys the system. Redwood provides:
- The same policy concepts (where applicable)
- Operational guidance, but the customer controls the physical/virtual location

---

## Compliance & evidence
### Q: What artifacts can we provide for audits / security questionnaires?
**A:** Common artifacts include:
- Data residency policy and controls narrative
- Architecture overview describing enforcement boundaries
- Audit log examples showing residency policy change events
- Screenshots or exports from dashboards showing blocked requests metrics (redacted)

Coordinate with GRC (Olga Petrov) for approved auditor-facing packages.

### Q: Does region pinning support SOC 2 / ISO 27001 narratives?
**A:** Yes. The feature is designed to map to common control expectations: access control, change management (audit logs), monitoring, and policy enforcement.

---

## Customer troubleshooting (field playbook)
### Q: Customer enabled pinning and now requests are blocked. What should we check first?
**A:**
1) Confirm the configured **allowed region set** matches where the customer expects to run
2) Confirm the customer is using the correct **org/project** and API key
3) Ask for: `request_id`, timestamp, endpoint, and project ID
4) Check whether they configured a single region without capacity (recommend adding a second allowed region within the same residency boundary, e.g., `eu-west` + `eu-central`)

### Q: Customer claims requests are being served outside the pinned region. What’s our response?
**A:**
- Ask for evidence: request IDs, timestamps, observed region headers (if available), and relevant logs
- Escalate to SRE + Routing: treat as a severity-appropriate incident because it may indicate a policy enforcement bug

### Q: How should we position the trade-off between residency strictness and availability?
**A:** Use this framing:
- Strict residency policies may reduce failover options.
- Redwood prioritizes compliance by blocking instead of violating policy.
- If the customer needs both strict residency and higher availability, recommend:
  - Allowing multiple regions within the same residency boundary (e.g., multiple EU regions)
  - Dedicated capacity in-region

---

## Approved language snippets (for emails / questionnaires)
**1) One-liner**
“Redwood supports region pinning for Hosted API. When enabled, customer content is processed only in the configured allowed regions, and requests that would violate policy are blocked with a deterministic error (no silent cross-region failover).”

**2) Logging/telemetry**
“For pinned workloads, Redwood keeps content-bearing logs/traces within the allowed region boundary. Operational metrics are designed to avoid customer content and may be aggregated centrally for service health.”

**3) Fallback behavior**
“Cross-region fallback is disabled by default under residency pinning. Redwood may fall back only within the allowed region set; otherwise requests fail rather than violating residency policy.”

---

## Contacts / escalation
- Product (policy intent, customer commitments): **Naomi Feldman**
- Security Engineering (controls, threat model): **Marcus Lin**
- GRC / evidence / auditor packs: **Olga Petrov**
- Solutions Engineering (customer rollout planning): **Markus Klein**
- SRE (enforcement incidents / false positives): **Sean Gallagher**

If a customer requests contractual language, route to Legal/Deal Desk and include Security + Product on the thread.",

    "title": "Introduce data-residency-guards, KMS key scoping, and RBAC v2 role mapping",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/github",
    "content": "{\n  \"repo\": \"redwood\",\n  \"pr_number\": \"86107\",\n  \"title\": \"Introduce data-residency-guards, KMS key scoping, and RBAC v2 role mapping\",\n  \"author\": \"Maya Chen\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-14\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-03-02\",\n  \"merged_at\": \"2026-03-02\",\n  \"state\": \"merged\",\n  \"base_branch\": \"main\",\n  \"head_branch\": \"feature/security/data-residency-kms-rbac-v2\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Luca Rivera\",\n    \"Priya Nair\",\n    \"Owen Park\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"security\",\n    \"compliance\",\n    \"rbac\",\n    \"kms\",\n    \"audit\",\n    \"privacy\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_linear\": [\n    \"ENG-4821\",\n    \"SEC-134\",\n    \"PM-210\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_jira\": [\n    \"SUP-7890\"\n  ],\n  \"ci_status\": \"pass\",\n  \"files_changed_count\": \"18\",\n  \"additions\": \"1128\",\n  \"deletions\": \"312\",\n  \"breaking_change\": \"false\",\n  \"release_notes\": \"Tenant-scoped KMS enforcement and data-residency guards; RBAC v2 mapping now honors region tags; audit header validation for routed requests; migration tool for existing customer KMS bindings.\",\n  \"description\": \"Summary: This PR implements tenant-aware data residency controls (aka 'residency-guards'), scopes KMS key usage to tenant+region, and extends RBAC v2 role mappings to carry region annotations. Motivation: Several enterprise customers requested hard guarantees that keys and audit streams remain in-customer regions and that role grants cannot be used to bypass residency rules. This change closes gaps discovered during compliance reviews and a recent support investigation (SUP-7890). High level changes: 1) Residency guard middleware: routes requests by tenant geo-tag and enforces region pinning policies; rejects or routes to fallback when policy mismatch. 2) KMS scoping: KMS key references now require a tenant and region qualifier; server-side validation added to key lookup path and crypto plugins updated to reject cross-region key usage. 3) RBAC v2 mapping: role mappings accept an optional region_claim attribute which restricts tokens to the specified region; evaluation engine updated to intersect tenant region and role region. 4) Audit propagation: introduced X-Redwood-Audit-Region header enforcement and enriched audit log entries with region and key_id. 5) Migration tooling: included kms-region-migrate script that converts legacy key bindings and emits a report for customer review. 6) Tests & CI: new unit and integration tests including simulated multi-region tenants and negative tests for mis-scoped keys. Commits (high level): - 2a1f7bd: residency guard middleware and policy model - 7b4e2c1: KMS validation and plugin API changes - 9c2d5f8: RBAC v2 evaluator region handling and mapping docs - d45a8e3: audit header enforcement and log enrichment - f1b9c02: kms-region-migrate tool and migration tests - 0e3a91d: add e2e scenarios to private installer suite Changed areas/files (high level): - src/security/residency/guard.go: new middleware and policy loader - proto/policy/residency.proto: policy schema additions - internal/kms/provider.go: key scoping and validation logic (illustrative snippet: if key.Region != request.Region { return ErrRegionMismatch }) - services/authn/rbac/v2/mapping.go: region_claim checks and eval updates - cmd/kms-region-migrate/main.go: migration entrypoint and report exporter - infra/priv-installer/e2e/residency_test.go: e2e scenarios for on-prem installer - docs/security/data-residency.md: design and operator runbook Review notes and conversation: - Priya: \\\"Can we ensure the middleware short-circuits before any key material is fetched?\\\" Author reply: \\\"Yes, guard checks run in the request admission path; added unit test and comment to make ordering explicit.\\\" - Luca: \\\"Migration tool looks good, but add a dry-run mode and a CSV report.\\\" Author reply: \\\"Added --dry-run and CSV output; report includes before/after key bindings.\\\" - Owen: \\\"What happens if a region label is missing on older tenants?\\\" Author reply: \\\"Policy default is inbound: tenants without explicit region remain in 'unscoped' bucket and are blocked from KMS operations until migration; we added an operator-facing migration guide.\\\" - Priya requested a security review for crypto plugin changes, later approved after one minor naming nit. CI: initial runs failed on lint due to naming of a test variable; fixed in follow-up commit and all checks passed (unit, integration, e2e). Performance: small runtime overhead for residency checks (~0.6ms median per request in microbench), measured in tests and within SLO for targeted customers. Backwards compatibility: the KMS provider API introduces a non-breaking optional parameter for region; we included shims in legacy adapters. Migration: kms-region-migrate included and tested; migration has to be scheduled by operator and can be rolled back by restoring previous binding snapshot. Security considerations: added threat mitigation section to docs and required an ACL check prior to migration script execution. Merge details: PR approved by reviewers and merged via squash on 2026-03-02. Squash commit message: \\\"security: add data-residency guards, KMS scoping, RBAC v2 region mapping\\\" Follow-ups: - ENG-4821: rollout plan for Dedicated clusters and Private installer upgrades - SEC-134: audit rule to alert on any requests rejected by residency guard - PM-210: UI controls to show tenant region and migration status in console Known limitations: cross-region read-only audit streams are not migrated automatically; operator action required. Notes for release: this change should be rolled out to staging + canary before full prod; include operators on migration schedule. Related: references SUP-7890 and internal design doc link: https://linear.app/redwood/doc/RESIDENCY-DESIGN (internal).\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"release_notes\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_dc53eb164da14c6ca5fe90eadc134e11\"\n}",

document.title: Introduce data-residency-guards, KMS key scoping, and RBAC v2 role mapping
document.content:
{
  "repo": "redwood",
  "pr_number": "86107",
  "title": "Introduce data-residency-guards, KMS key scoping, and RBAC v2 role mapping",
  "author": "Maya Chen",
  "created_at": "2026-02-14",
  "updated_at": "2026-03-02",
  "merged_at": "2026-03-02",
  "state": "merged",
  "base_branch": "main",
  "head_branch": "feature/security/data-residency-kms-rbac-v2",
  "reviewers": [
    "Luca Rivera",
    "Priya Nair",
    "Owen Park"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "security",
    "compliance",
    "rbac",
    "kms",
    "audit",
    "privacy"
  ],
  "linked_linear": [
    "ENG-4821",
    "SEC-134",
    "PM-210"
  ],
  "linked_jira": [
    "SUP-7890"
  ],
  "ci_status": "pass",
  "files_changed_count": "18",
  "additions": "1128",
  "deletions": "312",
  "breaking_change": "false",
  "release_notes": "Tenant-scoped KMS enforcement and data-residency guards; RBAC v2 mapping now honors region tags; audit header validation for routed requests; migration tool for existing customer KMS bindings.",
  "description": "Summary: This PR implements tenant-aware data residency controls (aka 'residency-guards'), scopes KMS key usage to tenant+region, and extends RBAC v2 role mappings to carry region annotations. Motivation: Several enterprise customers requested hard guarantees that keys and audit streams remain in-customer regions and that role grants cannot be used to bypass residency rules. This change closes gaps discovered during compliance reviews and a recent support investigation (SUP-7890). High level changes: 1) Residency guard middleware: routes requests by tenant geo-tag and enforces region pinning policies; rejects or routes to fallback when policy mismatch. 2) KMS scoping: KMS key references now require a tenant and region qualifier; server-side validation added to key lookup path and crypto plugins updated to reject cross-region key usage. 3) RBAC v2 mapping: role mappings accept an optional region_claim attribute which restricts tokens to the specified region; evaluation engine updated to intersect tenant region and role region. 4) Audit propagation: introduced X-Redwood-Audit-Region header enforcement and enriched audit log entries with region and key_id. 5) Migration tooling: included kms-region-migrate script that converts legacy key bindings and emits a report for customer review. 6) Tests & CI: new unit and integration tests including simulated multi-region tenants and negative tests for mis-scoped keys. Commits (high level): - 2a1f7bd: residency guard middleware and policy model - 7b4e2c1: KMS validation and plugin API changes - 9c2d5f8: RBAC v2 evaluator region handling and mapping docs - d45a8e3: audit header enforcement and log enrichment - f1b9c02: kms-region-migrate tool and migration tests - 0e3a91d: add e2e scenarios to private installer suite Changed areas/files (high level): - src/security/residency/guard.go: new middleware and policy loader - proto/policy/residency.proto: policy schema additions - internal/kms/provider.go: key scoping and validation logic (illustrative snippet: if key.Region != request.Region { return ErrRegionMismatch }) - services/authn/rbac/v2/mapping.go: region_claim checks and eval updates - cmd/kms-region-migrate/main.go: migration entrypoint and report exporter - infra/priv-installer/e2e/residency_test.go: e2e scenarios for on-prem installer - docs/security/data-residency.md: design and operator runbook Review notes and conversation: - Priya: \"Can we ensure the middleware short-circuits before any key material is fetched?\" Author reply: \"Yes, guard checks run in the request admission path; added unit test and comment to make ordering explicit.\" - Luca: \"Migration tool looks good, but add a dry-run mode and a CSV report.\" Author reply: \"Added --dry-run and CSV output; report includes before/after key bindings.\" - Owen: \"What happens if a region label is missing on older tenants?\" Author reply: \"Policy default is inbound: tenants without explicit region remain in 'unscoped' bucket and are blocked from KMS operations until migration; we added an operator-facing migration guide.\" - Priya requested a security review for crypto plugin changes, later approved after one minor naming nit. CI: initial runs failed on lint due to naming of a test variable; fixed in follow-up commit and all checks passed (unit, integration, e2e). Performance: small runtime overhead for residency checks (~0.6ms median per request in microbench), measured in tests and within SLO for targeted customers. Backwards compatibility: the KMS provider API introduces a non-breaking optional parameter for region; we included shims in legacy adapters. Migration: kms-region-migrate included and tested; migration has to be scheduled by operator and can be rolled back by restoring previous binding snapshot. Security considerations: added threat mitigation section to docs and required an ACL check prior to migration script execution. Merge details: PR approved by reviewers and merged via squash on 2026-03-02. Squash commit message: \"security: add data-residency guards, KMS scoping, RBAC v2 region mapping\" Follow-ups: - ENG-4821: rollout plan for Dedicated clusters and Private installer upgrades - SEC-134: audit rule to alert on any requests rejected by residency guard - PM-210: UI controls to show tenant region and migration status in console Known limitations: cross-region read-only audit streams are not migrated automatically; operator action required. Notes for release: this change should be rolled out to staging + canary before full prod; include operators on migration schedule. Related: references SUP-7890 and internal design doc link: https://linear.app/redwood/doc/RESIDENCY-DESIGN (internal).",

  "content_field_names": [
    "description",
    "release_notes"
  ],

}
